plot_extraction.response_text:
A magazine editor named Brown champions strict realism and discovers an ideal contributor in Robert Severne, a humorless young writer who insists on personally witnessing or experiencing everything he describes. Severne’s equally serious fiancée, Lucy Melville, prefers romantic fiction and breaks their engagement, promising forgiveness only if he publishes an imaginative story. Refusing to betray his artistic principles, Severne retreats to Wyoming to brood and gather realistic material.

While writing a Western, Severne realizes he has never experienced being chased by armed men. He hires several cowboys to pursue him with blank cartridges, but another group mistakes the chase for the pursuit of a horse thief and joins in with live ammunition. They kill his horse, capture him, dismiss his truthful explanation as an extravagant lie, and nearly hang him before the original cowboys arrive and rescue him.

Severne uses the ordeal to complete what he considers his most realistic masterpiece. Brown rejects it because the chase and the hero’s terror seem impossibly exaggerated and imaginative, but another magazine publishes it. Lucy reads the story without initially noticing the author’s name and concludes that Severne has written a brilliant romance to win her back. She returns, moved by what she believes is his loving sacrifice of principle. Though Severne knows the story is entirely realistic, he abandons the impulse to correct her when their reconciliation becomes romantic.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts a comic, satirical mode built around irony, exaggeration, and the repeated collision between literary theory and lived experience. Its central conceit is that Severne’s fanatical commitment to realism produces events so extraordinary that everyone interprets his truthful account as romantic invention. The narrative continually exposes the absurdity of rigid artistic principles, while also mocking editorial dogma, romantic self-dramatisation, Western conventions, and the solemnity of writers who take themselves too seriously.

The narrator is omniscient, intrusive, and conversational. Rather than remaining invisible, the narrative voice comments directly on characters and events, offers mock generalisations about editors, writers, lovers, girls, and serious-minded youths, and occasionally confesses uncertainty about minor details. Remarks such as uncertainty over whether the setting is a “dark gorge” or “narrow canon” deliberately puncture narrative authority and turn storytelling itself into part of the joke. The narrator often addresses the reader through phrases such as “you must see” and “conceive,” creating the atmosphere of an amused raconteur sharing a comic anecdote. This voice remains detached enough to recognise every character’s folly, but it is genial rather than cruel.

The prose alternates between brisk, declarative sentences and longer passages of mock-elevated exposition. Short sequences—“He glanced the story through. Then he read it carefully.”—create comic timing and imitate the “short, crisp sentences” praised within the story. Elsewhere, elaborate syntax parodies sentimental, philosophical, or melodramatic writing. Elevated formulations about martyrdom, shattered lives, noble sacrifice, and applauding angels are placed beside mundane realities such as bad hotel breakfasts, office clutter, fountain-pen maintenance, and sticky oatmeal. This contrast between grand rhetoric and trivial fact is one of the style’s principal comic mechanisms.

The diction is eclectic. Plain narration and colloquial phrasing coexist with deliberately pompous abstractions, literary terminology, Western slang, and mock-scientific comparisons. Words and phrases such as “poetic connotation,” “symbolical truth,” “Nebular Hypothesis,” and “perperoid lucubrations” caricature intellectual pretension, while dialect forms such as “pards,” “cayuse,” “ketched,” and “yore” establish the Western setting and sharpen the cultural contrast between Severne and the cowboys. Adjectives and descriptive formulas are frequently repeated—especially “short and crisp,” “served hot,” “serious-minded,” and “no sense of humour”—so that they become comic refrains.

Characterisation is largely caricatural and organised around governing traits. Brown is the dogmatic editor who worships realism; Severne is seriousness without perspective; Lucy is an equally doctrinaire romanticist; and the Westerners operate according to their own practical but mistaken assumptions. Psychological subtlety is less important than the escalating consequences of these fixed dispositions. Severne’s lack of humour is repeated so insistently that it becomes both the explanation for the plot and a running joke. His inward life is presented through mock-heroic fantasies in which ordinary disappointment becomes martyrdom, cosmic sacrifice, or the wreckage from which a monumental work of art will someday arise.

Dialogue is lively, theatrical, and strongly differentiated by social type. Brown speaks in editorial manifestos, Lucy in impassioned romantic declarations, Severne in grave abstractions, and the cowboys in compressed vernacular. Conversations often proceed as comic debates in which no participant truly understands the others. The dialogue also generates dramatic irony: readers recognise the absurd implications of Severne’s statements while the characters interpret them according to their own prejudices. Exclamation marks, interruptions, emphatic repetitions, and quick exchanges give confrontations a farcical energy.

The plot is tightly constructed through escalation and reversal. It begins as literary satire, shifts into romantic disagreement, expands into a parody of the Western adventure, and returns to the publishing world for the final ironic resolution. Recurring phrases and ideas provide cohesion: realism, imagination, crisp sentences, hot adjectives, poetic connotation, and Severne’s solemnity reappear in altered contexts. The staged pursuit becomes real; the resulting truthful story is rejected as implausible by the realist editor; it is accepted elsewhere as fiction; and Lucy reads it as proof that Severne has abandoned realism for her sake. Each reversal grows logically from the characters’ misconceptions.

Pacing varies according to comic purpose. Expository passages rapidly summarise Severne’s career, beliefs, and courtship, while the chase and attempted hanging are narrated in more immediate, sequential detail. Even during danger, the narrator sustains a light tone through understatement and incongruity. Hanging is treated with grotesque casualness, and Severne’s near death is framed as an unusually rich supply of “realistic experience.” Violence therefore functions less as tragedy than as farcical escalation, though its genuine peril intensifies the absurdity.

The story is highly metafictional. It discusses how stories should be written, edited, judged, typed, sold, and interpreted while simultaneously demonstrating competing styles. Its realism is itself stylised, its Western episode uses recognisable adventure conventions, and its romantic conclusion depends on a misunderstanding about genre. The text repeatedly suggests that “reality” in fiction is determined not simply by factual truth but by plausibility, expectation, and the reader’s interpretive frame. Art and life mirror and distort one another until a perfectly accurate account appears imaginary.

The ending condenses the story’s method into a final comic surrender. Severne briefly sees an obligation to defend the truth and preserve his artistic principles, but romantic opportunity defeats theoretical consistency. The closing question—“And Art; oh, where was it?”—is mock-tragic, rhetorical, and self-consciously literary. It leaves the story on an ironic note: artistic dogma has vanished not through reasoned conversion, but through desire, timing, and a kiss. Overall, the style is urbane, playful, episodic, and self-aware, with humour arising from deadpan narration, mock grandeur, verbal repetition, social caricature, and carefully prepared reversals.

generation.response_text:
# The Extreme Realist

I

When Mr. Horace Brown became editor of *The Metropolitan Monthly*, he found upon his desk seven hundred and forty-three manuscripts, a blue pencil, three unpaid luncheon bills, and the conviction that American literature was dying of imagination.

The manuscripts had accumulated under the former editor, who had possessed a tender heart and weak eyesight. Brown disposed of both the manuscripts and the former editor’s principles within a week.

“What the public wants,” he announced, “is Reality.”

He pronounced the word with a capital letter. Editors can do this orally. It is one of their privileges, and partly accounts for their salaries.

“No more dreams,” said Brown. “No more palaces on coral islands. No more clever young dukes disguised as gardeners. No more women whose eyes resemble moonlight upon deep water. Have you ever seen an eye that resembled moonlight upon deep water?”

His assistant, Ferris, admitted that he had not.

“Exactly! Eyes are eyes. Water is water. Moonlight is moonlight. The business of literature is to keep them separate.”

Ferris made a note of this. He made notes of everything Brown said, though he afterward used the backs of them for calculating postage.

Brown’s ideal story must be true to life, short and crisp, served hot, and devoid of poetic connotation. Especially poetic connotation. He had once rejected a very good tale because the author had spoken of a “weary road.” Roads, Brown explained, possessed no nervous system and could not become weary.

He prohibited sunsets unless the author supplied the precise meteorological conditions. He discouraged love at first sight because, statistically, it so often led to regret. He objected to villains, holding that no human being was wholly bad, although he sometimes forgot this doctrine when discussing rival editors. He demanded that every story deal with things the author knew personally.

“Write what you have lived,” was his motto. “If you have lived nothing, do not write. Get a position in wholesale groceries.”

His office reflected his creed. There were no flowers in it, because flowers suggested spring, youth, burial, marriage, and other poetic connotations. There were two steel filing cabinets, a roll-top desk, a calendar advertising kidney pills, and an umbrella which belonged to nobody. On the wall hung a framed notice:

FACTS FIRST.  
ADJECTIVES HOT.  
SENTENCES SHORT AND CRISP.

What was meant by hot adjectives neither Brown nor anyone else precisely knew, but the phrase had energy.

For six months Brown searched for an author who would embody his principles. He found men who wrote from life, but unfortunately they had led no life worth writing about. He found men who had led remarkable lives, but they could not spell. He found one sailor who had been shipwrecked eleven times and who submitted an article entitled “The Ocean’s Call.” Brown rejected it because the ocean did not call; it merely moved under gravitational and atmospheric influences.

Then Robert Severne appeared.

Severne was twenty-seven, pale, thin, upright, and serious-minded. He had large gray eyes, a careful necktie, and no sense of humour. I do not mean that his sense of humour was undeveloped, misdirected, or asleep. He had none. A joke entered his mind as a fly enters a bottle: it buzzed briefly against transparent obstacles and died.

He laid a manuscript upon Brown’s desk.

“Is this drawn from personal experience?” asked Brown.

“Entirely,” said Severne.

Brown glanced through the story. Then he read it carefully. Then he shut the office door and read it again.

It concerned a bookkeeper who missed his suburban train, ate a bad dinner at a railway restaurant, and arrived home to discover that the kitchen pipe had burst. There was no murder, no mystery, no hidden will, and no woman with violet eyes. The pipe was repaired by a plumber who charged three dollars and seventy-five cents. Severne had paid precisely that sum.

“It is magnificent,” said Brown.

“It is accurate,” said Severne.

“Better! The descriptions are photographs.”

“I measured the restaurant.”

“The dialogue is life itself.”

“I took notes.”

“The oatmeal—how did you achieve that extraordinary passage about the oatmeal?”

“I ate it.”

Brown rose and clasped his hand.

“My boy,” he said, “you are the man American literature has been waiting for.”

American literature, which had not been consulted, continued to wait with considerable composure.

II

From that day Robert Severne became the prophet of the New Realism, although he earned only forty dollars a story and frequently had to borrow carfare. Brown printed his tales under titles such as “Tuesday,” “A Visit to the Dentist,” and “The Second Floor Back.” Critics praised their restraint. One of them declared that Severne had exposed the colossal tragedy latent in the ordinary boiled potato. Severne wrote to the critic asking what tragedy he meant.

He was incapable of describing anything he had not personally seen, heard, tasted, touched, measured, or suffered. If a character caught cold, Severne sat in a draft until he sneezed. Before writing of a clerk dismissed by his employer, he obtained temporary employment in a haberdashery and contrived to insult the proprietor. For a story about insomnia, he drank nine cups of coffee and spent the night counting cracks in the ceiling.

He once began a tale in which a man was stung by a bee. Halfway through the opening paragraph, his conscience stopped him. He had never been stung by a bee.

For three afternoons he visited parks carrying a pot of honey. The bees ignored him. On the fourth day a wasp supplied the required sensation, but Severne discarded the paragraph because a wasp was not a bee and the pain might possess an entirely different literary value.

Brown adored him.

“Integrity!” he cried. “That is integrity. The average writer would change the bee into a wasp. Or, worse, leave it a bee and trust to imagination. Imagination is the bankruptcy court of observation.”

Severne agreed. He always agreed gravely. Brown might have said that the Nebular Hypothesis was responsible for weak characterisation, and Severne would have considered the claim before accepting it in principle.

Now, there was in Severne’s life a young woman named Lucy Melville.

Why a young woman had entered it is one of those mysteries with which nature confounds philosophy. Lucy was pretty, dark-haired, serious-minded, and devoted to romantic fiction. She had no more sense of humour than Severne, but hers was a different sort of humourlessness. Severne took facts seriously; Lucy took emotions seriously. He believed a thing noble if it had occurred. She believed it noble if it could not possibly occur.

Her favourite novels contained ruined abbeys, ancestral curses, masked horsemen, secret marriages, hereditary jewels, and young men who renounced kingdoms for governesses. The men in them had proud lips and incurable sorrows. They seldom worked. Their hearts broke with astonishing regularity, but their health remained excellent through four hundred pages.

Severne loved Lucy because she had soft eyes and listened when he discussed technique. Lucy loved Severne because his silence seemed full of suffering. It was actually full of punctuation, but silence permits generous interpretations.

They became engaged on a Sunday afternoon beneath an elm tree.

“I have never before asked a woman to marry me,” said Severne.

Lucy’s eyes filled.

“That makes it beautiful.”

“It makes it accurate.”

“And you will love me always?”

“I can make no statement concerning future emotional conditions without sufficient data.”

She accepted this as a solemn delicacy of feeling and leaned her head upon his shoulder.

Their engagement proceeded peacefully until Lucy began reading Severne’s stories.

At first she tried to admire them. Love can do much. It can make a girl praise a man’s poetry, endure his friends, and pretend not to notice that he eats asparagus incorrectly. But love could not make Lucy admire “The Burst Kitchen Pipe.”

“Robert,” she said one evening, “does nothing ever happen in your stories?”

“Everything happens exactly as it happened.”

“But nobody sacrifices anything.”

“In ‘The Insurance Premium,’ Wilkins sacrifices thirty-eight dollars and ten cents.”

“For love, I mean.”

“His insurance was for his wife’s benefit.”

Lucy pressed one hand to her forehead.

“You do not understand. I mean a great sacrifice. A man should cast away ambition, fortune, perhaps honour itself, for the woman he loves.”

“That would be criminally improvident.”

“He should cross deserts for her.”

“Unless she had chosen to reside in a desert, the journey would be unnecessary.”

“He should face death!”

“I see no practical connection between death and matrimony.”

Lucy stared at him. The lamp burned low. Outside, rain whispered against the windows, though Severne afterward maintained that it struck them at an average angle of forty degrees and made a sound more like tapping.

“Robert,” she said, “have you ever imagined anything?”

“No.”

“Never?”

“Not deliberately.”

She rose.

“Then you cannot love.”

This was unjust, but admirably romantic.

Severne also rose.

“My pulse increases measurably in your presence.”

“Pulse!” cried Lucy. “You speak to me of pulse!”

“It is accepted physiological evidence of emotion.”

“A thermometer could love me by your standards.”

“A thermometer does not possess a pulse.”

That finished it.

Lucy removed her engagement ring. It caught at the knuckle, which somewhat impaired the majesty of the act, but after a brief struggle she placed it on the table.

“You must choose,” she said. “Your creed—or me.”

“My creed is truth.”

“And I am romance?”

“You have frequently expressed a preference for it.”

“Then write one story for me. One story of imagination. Invent something splendid, impossible, heroic. Let a man suffer for love. Let him ride through danger. Let him risk his life. Publish it under your own name, and I shall know you have sacrificed your principles for my sake.”

Severne became pale. A lesser man might have lied, but he would first have needed to imagine the lie, and Severne was helpless.

“You ask me,” he said, “to prostitute Art.”

Lucy put on her cloak.

“I ask you to prove that you love me.”

“There should be another method.”

“There is none.”

“Could I expose myself to influenza?”

“No.”

“Lose money?”

“No.”

“Remain awake for forty-eight hours?”

“No!”

She moved toward the door, then paused in the soft light, her cloak falling about her like the mantle of outraged Romance.

“When you have written an imaginative story,” she said, “come to me. Until then, everything is over.”

The door closed.

Severne stood motionless.

The lamp smoked. The ring lay on the table. Somewhere a clock struck nine, though possibly it was ten; the narrator was not present with a notebook. Severne’s soul surveyed the wreckage of its universe.

Then he sat down and recorded the conversation while it was fresh.

III

Brown received news of the broken engagement with professional enthusiasm.

“Excellent!” he said. “Suffering is material.”

Severne looked wounded.

“I have lost the woman I love.”

“Precisely. Get it down at once. Short and crisp.”

“It is not a subject for fiction.”

“My dear boy, everything is a subject for fiction after it has become sufficiently painful.”

Severne walked to the window. Below him the city roared, surged, thundered, murmured, or merely conducted traffic; choose the verb according to your school of literature.

“She believes imagination superior to truth,” he said.

“Women do.”

“All women?”

“Every woman who has rejected a manuscript of mine.”

“I must go away.”

“Where?”

“Somewhere primitive. Somewhere emotion is stripped of artificial conventions. Somewhere I may observe fundamental realities.”

“Wyoming,” said Brown.

“Why Wyoming?”

Brown pointed to a railroad advertisement on the opposite wall. It displayed a cowboy galloping beneath the words THE REAL WEST AWAITS YOU.

“There,” said Brown, “you have documentary evidence.”

Thus it happened that Robert Severne journeyed west with two trunks, a typewriter, a folding ruler, six notebooks, and a grief which he believed eternal. Young men commonly mistake the duration of grief. So do widows, poets, and persons with toothache.

He found lodging on a cattle ranch belonging to a broad, weathered man named Ike Mangum. Ike wore leather chaps, spoke sparingly, and regarded the typewriter as a machine designed to frighten horses.

“What you figger on doin’ with that contraption?” he asked.

“I write stories.”

Ike considered.

“True ones?”

“Entirely.”

“Then why write ’em?”

The question troubled Severne for several days.

Ranch life supplied abundant material. He learned to saddle a horse, mend a fence, brand a calf, distinguish between several kinds of dust, and eat beans without expectation. He recorded everything. If Ike said, “Mornin’,” Severne wrote it down. If a cow looked at him, he described the expression, then revised the description because he could not establish what the cow had intended.

At night he sat in his room over the ranch kitchen and worked beneath a smoky lamp. The room contained a bed, a chair, a cracked basin, and one energetic mosquito. Its window looked toward plains so enormous that even Severne felt something resembling poetic connotation. He fought it.

His sorrow deepened—or, more accurately, became organised. He pictured Lucy reading of his lonely exile. He imagined—no, he did not imagine; he deduced—that future generations would revere him as the martyr of Realism. Critics would speak of “the Wyoming period,” during which privation burned away his last concessions to popular taste. There might be a monument. On one side would stand Truth, austere and possibly bronze. On the other would sit Love, veiled and remorseful.

These reflections comforted him, although they were perilously imaginative.

After three months he began a Western story.

It concerned a young ranch hand named John Smith who discovered irregularities in the ranch accounts, mentioned them to the foreman, and was discharged. Severne had personally inspected accounts and been discharged from a haberdashery, so the foundation was firm. But Brown had lately written that readers desired “movement.”

“Give me action,” Brown said. “Not imaginary action, naturally. Real action. Served hot.”

Severne therefore arranged for John Smith to be chased by armed men.

He wrote the opening of the episode.

John mounted his horse and fled. Behind him came four riders, firing as they rode. Bullets struck the earth near his horse’s hoofs. He experienced considerable fear.

Severne stopped.

“Considerable fear” was vague. Worse, it was dishonest. He had never been pursued by armed men. He did not know whether a fugitive heard separate shots or one continuous disturbance; whether he looked behind him; whether terror dried the throat, tightened the stomach, weakened the knees, or produced all three effects in alphabetical order. He had never felt a bullet pass near his head. He could not continue.

For an ordinary writer, this difficulty would have lasted the time required to sharpen a pencil. For Severne it became a moral crisis.

He consulted Ike.

“I require four men to chase me on horseback,” he said.

Ike removed a splinter from his thumb.

“What for?”

“Art.”

“Art who?”

“My work. I must ascertain the sensations of pursuit.”

Ike thought this over.

“You been drinkin’?”

“No.”

“Snake-bit?”

“No.”

“Woman trouble?”

Severne stiffened.

“That is irrelevant.”

“Then it’s a woman.”

Eventually Ike consented to help, partly from good nature and partly because cowboys living fifty miles from a railway welcome any entertainment not involving a broken leg. Four ranch hands volunteered: Pete Givens, Shorty Bale, Mexican Sam, who was from Illinois, and a youth called Deacon because he had once attended church.

The plan was simple. Severne would ride away with a five-minute start. The others would pursue him for ten miles, shout threats, and fire blank cartridges. At Black Tooth Ravine they would overtake him. Severne would then record his sensations while hot, short, and crisp.

“Don’t shoot too close,” Ike warned.

“We ain’t shootin’ nothin’,” said Pete. “Blanks.”

“Don’t get excited and forget.”

“Who, us?”

Ike looked at them. The question answered itself.

The experiment began at two in the afternoon.

Severne wore a dark coat because John Smith wore one in the manuscript. He carried a notebook in his breast pocket and a pencil attached to his wrist by string. Before mounting, he inspected the blank cartridges.

“You understand,” he said, “that your expressions must be authentic but not personally offensive.”

“What kin we call you?” asked Shorty.

“Anything a pursuer would naturally call a fugitive.”

Shorty brightened.

“No references to Miss Melville,” Severne added.

The cowboys exchanged disappointed glances.

Severne rode out across the plain.

Five minutes later the others followed, whooping magnificently and discharging their revolvers into the air. Their horses sprang forward. Dust rose. Birds flew from the sagebrush. A distant herd of cattle reached the conclusion that civilisation had again failed and moved elsewhere.

At first Severne felt self-conscious. He noted that the shots were distinct, that his horse’s hoofbeats seemed louder than usual, and that glancing backward at speed endangered balance. He wrote these facts while riding.

Then a blank charge scorched the brim of his hat.

His observations became less academic.

“Mind the distance!” he shouted.

“Ride, you thievin’ skunk!” bawled Pete, entering into his part.

Severne’s horse accelerated. The plain rolled beneath him. Wind tore at his eyes. The pursuing cries came closer, then receded, then spread strangely to the north.

This last phenomenon required explanation.

A second party of cowboys had appeared beyond a low ridge. They were seven in number and belonged to the Bar Circle outfit. That morning someone had stolen a bay horse from their remuda. Coming upon four armed men pursuing a pale stranger in a dark coat, they instantly understood the situation. Cowboys, like editors and lovers, understand situations most completely when they understand them wrong.

“There he goes!” shouted their leader, Bud Ransome.

“Horse thief!” yelled another.

They joined the chase.

Pete saw them coming.

“Company,” he remarked.

“What they want?” asked Mexican Sam.

“Reckon they want in.”

“Wave ’em off.”

Pete waved. The Bar Circle men interpreted the gesture as an appeal for assistance and came faster.

Severne glanced back and saw eleven riders instead of four.

His first thought was that Ike had enlarged the experiment without permission. His second was that this constituted a serious breach of artistic method. His third was interrupted by the crack of a rifle and the sharp, vicious sound of a bullet passing within a foot of his ear.

A blank cartridge does not make that sound.

Severne’s scalp tightened. His mouth became dry. His stomach appeared to remove itself from its customary location. Here, at last, was exact information, but he felt no satisfaction.

Another shot struck the ground ahead of him and threw dust into his face.

“Stop shootin’!” cried Pete.

“Spread out!” shouted Bud Ransome.

The two commands reached Severne as one long howl.

His horse, which had entered into the spirit of realism more completely than its rider, stretched flat and ran. Sagebrush whipped by. The land fell into a shallow valley and rose toward a line of broken hills. Severne clung to the saddle and discovered that a man under fire does not think noble thoughts. He does not review his childhood. He does not forgive his enemies. He thinks chiefly of getting behind something thick.

He also discovered that fear was not “considerable.” It was enormous, cold, intimate, and humiliating. It occupied his boots. It trembled in his fingers. It made the sky too bright and every stone offensively distinct.

A bullet struck his canteen.

Water streamed down his leg.

He had time to think, with indignation, that readers would consider this symbolical.

Then his horse stumbled.

There was a thud, a violent turning of earth and sky, and the astonishing fact of ground against his cheek. The horse rolled away, kicked twice, and lay still. Severne rose on one knee. His pencil string had wrapped itself around his thumb. His notebook had vanished.

The riders closed in.

“Hands up!” cried Bud.

Severne raised them.

Pete and the other hired pursuers had pulled up fifty yards away. The Bar Circle men, seeing themselves superior in number and righteousness, covered everybody with rifles.

“Got him!” said one.

“I surrender,” Severne replied.

“Durn decent of you.”

“I wish to explain.”

“They all do,” said Bud.

IV

The Bar Circle party conducted Severne to a patch of cottonwoods beside a dry creek. Pete and his companions followed under guard, protesting with such richness of language that Severne, even in peril, regretted losing his notebook.

Bud Ransome was a tall man with narrow eyes and a red moustache. He possessed the solemn confidence of one who has never doubted a mistake.

“Where’s the hoss?” he demanded.

“My horse has been shot.”

“Not your cayuse. Our bay.”

“I know nothing of your bay.”

Bud looked at his companions.

“He knows nothin’.”

“That’s bad,” said one.

“Always is,” said another.

Pete pushed forward.

“Listen, pards. This here’s no hoss thief. He’s a writer.”

There was a pause.

The Bar Circle men looked at Severne with new suspicion.

“A what?”

“A story writer. He paid us to chase him.”

Bud turned slowly toward Severne.

“You paid four men to run you down and shoot at you?”

“With blank cartridges.”

“What for?”

“To acquire authentic experience for a work of fiction.”

The silence that followed was profound. A grasshopper made a brief statement and withdrew it.

Bud removed his hat and scratched his head.

“You mean to say,” he began patiently, “that you hired these yahoos to chase you across Wyoming so’s you could write how it felt?”

“Yes.”

“And that dark coat is for the story?”

“Yes.”

“And that there pencil tied to your hand?”

“Yes.”

“And you ain’t stole no bay?”

“No.”

Bud replaced his hat.

“Boys,” he said, “I’ve heard some lies.”

His companions nodded.

“I’ve heard whoppers that’d make a Missouri mule climb a tree to get away from ’em. But this—this has feathers.”

“It is the exact truth,” said Severne.

“That proves it,” said Bud. “No man tells the exact truth unless he’s fixin’ to sell somethin’.”

Pete attempted intervention.

“He’s plumb cracked on realism.”

“What’s realism?”

“Means he can’t write nothin’ till it’s happened to him.”

Bud stared.

“Then let’s hang him. He can write about that.”

The suggestion was received with approval.

Severne felt the cold fear return, but sharper. He drew himself up.

“You cannot execute a man upon an unsupported assumption.”

“We got support,” said Bud. “The bay’s gone, you’re runnin’, and them four are chasin’ you.”

“They were employed to chase me.”

“That’s the unsupported part.”

“It is corroborated by all four.”

“Four men in on a hoss theft can corroborate a heap.”

Shorty spat.

“You ain’t got sense enough to pour sand out of a boot.”

Bud levelled his rifle.

“Maybe not. But I got sense enough to make five men quiet.”

At this point Deacon began laughing. It was not prudent laughter, but cowboys do not always choose prudence, especially when it has been a long day.

“Quit that,” said Bud.

“I was just thinkin’,” Deacon gasped, “how Bob here’ll describe this. ‘The condemned man laughed short and crisp.’”

Even Severne might have perceived humour in the situation had he not been the condemned man.

The Bar Circle riders produced a rope. One end was thrown across the branch of a cottonwood. The action was accomplished with an efficiency which did not reassure Severne. Western men are often casual about hanging because they do not expect to be the noun in the sentence.

“You are committing murder,” he said.

“Mebbe,” replied Bud. “But we’re doin’ it realistic.”

They tied Severne’s hands.

Here the narrator ought perhaps to describe the dark gorge in which the cottonwoods stood. It may have been a narrow canon. Authorities differ as to the geological dignity required by such places. There were stones, a bank, some trees, and enough shade to make the proceedings picturesque, which was the very quality Severne had always distrusted.

The noose was placed around his neck.

Instantly he observed several facts. Rope scratched the skin. A man awaiting death heard trivial sounds with absurd clarity. One of the horses was chewing its bit. A Bar Circle rider had a loose spur. Bud smelled of tobacco. Clouds moved above the branches with an indifference that would have seemed poetic had it not been insulting.

Severne thought of Lucy.

This annoyed him. He had expected to think of artistic principle.

He saw her as she had stood in the lamplight, asking him to prove love by sacrifice. He saw the engagement ring on the table. He wondered whether dying for realism would count. Probably not. Lucy had rigid standards.

Bud took hold of the rope.

“Anything to say?”

“Yes,” said Severne. “The sensation produced by a noose is not primarily one of constriction. It is irritation at the left side of the neck, accompanied by—”

“Pull,” said someone.

There came a thunder of hoofs.

Ike Mangum burst over the bank with six ranch hands behind him. He had become uneasy when shooting continued too long and had ridden after the experiment. Unlike Severne, Ike did not require personal experience to infer trouble.

“Drop that rope!” he shouted.

Rifles swung. Men cursed. Horses wheeled. For ten lively seconds the air was crowded with commands, explanations, threats, dust, and hot adjectives.

Ike knew Bud Ransome. More importantly, he knew that the missing Bar Circle bay had been found an hour earlier, grazing contentedly in a draw after pushing through a broken fence.

Bud listened. His red moustache sagged.

“Found, you say?”

“Found.”

“Same bay?”

“How many bays you lose this mornin’?”

Bud looked at Severne, who still stood beneath the tree wearing the noose.

“Well,” he said, “that alters the case.”

“It does from here,” said Severne.

Bud untied him.

“No hard feelin’s.”

“I possess very hard feelings.”

“Natural. But you got to admit your yarn sounded uncommon.”

“It was true.”

“That’s what made it uncommon.”

Pete recovered the missing notebook near the dead horse. Severne found that his notes ended with the sentence: “When genuine bullets are introduced, terror increases abruptly.”

He underlined it twice.

V

For three weeks Severne wrote.

He wrote in the ranch house, on the porch, in bed, at meals, and once while Ike was explaining that the roof had caught fire. His Western story expanded beyond its original dimensions. John Smith was chased, shot at, captured, accused, threatened, and almost hanged. Every detail was exact. Severne measured the noose. He interviewed Bud concerning his state of mind. Bud claimed he had never had one, but supplied the dialect.

The sentences were short and crisp. The adjectives were served hot. There was no poetic connotation except where Lucy’s face had appeared to the hero under the cottonwoods; Severne deleted that passage and restored it four times.

At last the manuscript was complete.

He titled it “The Pursuit.”

“It is,” he told Ike, “the most realistic story ever written.”

Ike, repairing a cinch, grunted.

“Everything in it happened.”

“Too bad.”

“Why?”

“Makes it hard to believe.”

Severne pitied the limitations of an unliterary mind and sent the manuscript to Brown.

Then he waited.

He conceived Brown reading it in the office beneath FACTS FIRST. He saw the editor spring up, overturning the umbrella, and cry, “At last!” He foresaw a special issue, critical acclaim, perhaps an editorial manifesto. The story would establish Realism beyond dispute. Lucy might read it. She would be forced to recognise the majesty of truth, although he had no intention of taking her back unless she recanted fully and perhaps in writing.

He checked the mail twice a day.

Brown’s reply arrived in nine days.

It contained the manuscript.

> My dear Severne:
>
> I am deeply disappointed. What has happened to you? This story is impossible from beginning to end. The pursuit is theatrical, the accidental arrival of a second posse is an obvious device, the shooting of the horse is melodrama, and the attempted hanging exceeds every bound of probability.
>
> Most serious of all, the hero’s terror is grossly exaggerated. No human being notices his stomach changing location or the sky becoming offensively bright. These are imaginative flourishes, unworthy of your former method.
>
> I fear Wyoming has corrupted you. Return to observed life. Give me something quiet, true, short and crisp. A hotel breakfast, perhaps.
>
> Yours faithfully,  
> Horace Brown.

Severne read the letter. Then he read it carefully. Then he walked out behind the barn and uttered several expressions which were neither short nor crisp, though they were unquestionably hot.

He wrote Brown sixteen pages of explanation. He enclosed affidavits from Ike, Pete, Shorty, Mexican Sam, Deacon, Bud Ransome, and the owner of the dead horse. Brown returned the documents.

“Proof,” he wrote, “does not create plausibility.”

This sentence deserves preservation. It contains more editorial wisdom than Brown intended.

Severne’s universe collapsed for the second time that year. First Love had demanded Imagination. Now Realism demanded restraint from Reality. He had suffered for Art, and Art had sent the manuscript back with insufficient postage.

For two days he considered abandoning literature and entering wholesale groceries.

On the third day, in a gesture of despair, he mailed “The Pursuit” to *The Hearth and Home Companion*, a magazine famous for countesses, hidden treasure, noble bandits, and illustrations of men embracing women on staircases. Its editor, a cheerful woman named Miss Vale, accepted the story by return mail.

“Your extraordinary romance thrilled us,” she wrote. “The invention is audacious, the danger superbly unreal, and the emotional exaggeration exactly suited to our readers. We congratulate you upon abandoning the narrow photographic method of your earlier work.”

Severne received three hundred dollars.

This softened the blow without explaining it.

VI

Lucy Melville encountered “The Pursuit” in a railway waiting room.

She was travelling to visit an aunt who possessed bronchitis, money, and a large house near Albany. The train was late. Trains are frequently late in romantic circumstances, partly because Providence understands construction.

Lucy bought *The Hearth and Home Companion* but did not examine the table of contents. She began reading while seated beneath a clock that had stopped at twenty minutes past four.

The story seized her.

Here at last was life as Lucy preferred it: life purified of probability. A lonely horseman fled across a blazing plain. Armed riders thundered behind. Bullets sang. A horse fell. The hero faced unjust death beneath dark trees and, at the supreme instant, beheld the face of the woman he loved.

Lucy’s eyes filled with tears.

She read faster.

The sentences were short and crisp. The adjectives were served hot. The details possessed a strange vividness. Dust stung her own face. The rope seemed to scrape her own neck, though this may have been the tight collar then fashionable. Above all, she felt the sacrifice hidden in the work. Whoever had written it must have cast petty reason aside and surrendered himself to splendid invention.

She turned the last page and saw the name.

ROBERT SEVERNE.

The waiting room vanished. The clock, the delayed train, the aunt with bronchitis, and a child eating an orange ceased to exist. Lucy understood everything.

Robert had done it for her.

He had broken his creed. He had renounced the cold idol of Fact. He had invented a pursuit, a hail of bullets, a fallen horse, savage cowboys, and an impossible rescue. He had even allowed his hero, beneath the noose, to see the beloved woman’s face. No communication could have been clearer unless accompanied by a diagram.

“What a sacrifice!” she whispered.

The child with the orange stared at her.

Lucy rose. The Albany train arrived. She did not board it. Bronchitis, money, and a large house might wait; Love had issued a more dramatic timetable.

By evening she was travelling west.

Now, a less serious-minded girl might have written first. A girl with humour might have suspected complications. Lucy did neither. Her conception of reconciliation required distance, surprise, tears, forgiveness, and preferably a sunset. She intended to stand before Severne and say, “Robert, I understand.” After that, she trusted to his shattered heart.

Her journey occupied three days. During it she reread “The Pursuit” twelve times. Each reading enlarged the sacrifice. By Nebraska, Severne had not merely invented a story; he had crucified his artistic soul. By Cheyenne, angels were applauding.

She reached Ike Mangum’s ranch at six in the evening.

The sunset was available.

Severne sat on the porch repairing his fountain pen. A bottle of ink stood beside him. His collar was open, his hair untidy, and his expression that of a man who has discovered that Truth pays forty dollars while Romance pays three hundred.

He heard wheels. A ranch wagon stopped at the gate.

Lucy descended.

For once Severne’s powers of observation failed him. He rose so suddenly that he spilled ink upon his trousers.

“Lucy!”

“Robert!”

She came toward him across the yard.

Ike looked from one to the other, entered the house, and drove all the ranch hands out through the kitchen. He had no literary theories, but he possessed discretion.

Lucy stopped at the foot of the porch.

“I have read it,” she said.

Severne’s heart gave a violent beat. He noted this automatically.

“Read what?”

“Your story.”

“Oh.”

“The story you wrote for me.”

Severne opened his mouth.

Lucy continued, and there was no stopping her. Emotion had accumulated across seventeen hundred miles.

“I understand now. I understand what it cost you. Every impossible incident, every invented danger, every magnificent exaggeration was a renunciation. You trampled your principles underfoot for my sake.”

Severne’s mouth remained open.

“You sent your hero across the plain because I had asked for a man who would ride through danger. You put him beneath the rope because I had asked for a man who would face death. And at that final instant you made him see the woman he loved.”

“That detail—” Severne began.

“I knew! I knew it was meant for me.”

“It was based upon—”

“No, do not explain.” Lucy mounted the porch. “Explanations belong to the old Robert, the cold Robert, the man of measurements and affidavits. The new Robert has imagination.”

“There is no new Robert.”

“How like you to be modest.”

“I assure you, the story is wholly—”

She placed both hands in his.

You must see his difficulty.

On one side stood Truth: austere, naked, shivering slightly, and furnished with seven affidavits. On the other stood Lucy: warm, dark-eyed, repentant, and close enough to make physiological evidence unnecessary. Behind Truth stood Brown, returned manuscripts, bad hotel breakfasts, and a future in wholesale groceries. Behind Lucy stood forgiveness.

“I was wrong,” she said softly. “Love is greater than a creed.”

Severne looked into her eyes.

Somewhere in his mind Art rose, adjusted its robe, and demanded to be defended.

He ought to have told her everything. He ought to have described the blank cartridges, the second posse, the live bullets, the dead horse, the noose, and Bud Ransome’s red moustache. He ought to have produced the affidavits. He ought to have proclaimed that the impossible story was true, that strict realism had achieved its purest triumph, and that readers, editors, and fiancées were united in error.

He drew breath.

Lucy lifted her face.

Severne had personally experienced bullets, terror, unjust accusation, and the abrasion of rope. He had not, however, experienced this precise moment.

As an artist, he required data.

He kissed her.

The experiment lasted longer than was strictly necessary.

When they separated, Lucy whispered, “And you will never sacrifice love to Art again?”

Severne glanced toward the open window of his room. On the desk lay Brown’s rejection, Miss Vale’s acceptance, the marked manuscript, and the affidavits establishing the exact truth.

He considered making one final statement.

Then Lucy kissed him.

The statement was postponed.

And Art—Truthful, uncompromising, short and crisp, with all its adjectives served hot—Art, oh, where was it?

The Museum of Lost Hours

At precisely nine o’clock every morning, Elias Vale unlocked the brass doors of the Museum of Lost Hours.

The museum stood at the end of Bellweather Street, wedged between a bakery that sold burnt sugar cakes and a watchmaker whose clocks never agreed. It was a narrow, gray building with seven floors, though from the street it looked scarcely tall enough for three. Above the doors, carved into black stone, were the words:

WHAT IS LOST IS NOT ALWAYS GONE.

Most visitors assumed the museum displayed antique clocks. They entered expecting pendulums, sundials, and delicate silver pocket watches. There were some clocks, certainly, but they were not the purpose of the place.

The museum collected time people had lost.

On the first floor stood glass jars filled with wasted afternoons. They glowed faintly gold, like honey held up to the sun. On the second floor, locked in cedar cabinets, were years spent waiting for apologies that never came. The third floor contained childhood summers forgotten by those who had grown too quickly. Those were preserved in green bottles and smelled, when opened, of grass, rain, and warm dust.

The fourth floor was closed to the public.

So were the fifth, sixth, and seventh.

Elias had been the museum’s caretaker for forty-three years. He dusted the exhibits, polished the labels, and ensured that no visitor touched anything. Time, once separated from the person who had lived it, could be dangerous. A wasted minute might seem harmless, but minutes gathered in crowds. They slipped under doors, hid in sleeves, and occasionally attached themselves to strangers.

That was why the museum had rules.

Do not open the jars.

Do not speak your full name in the Gallery of Forgotten Birthdays.

Do not look into the clock with no hands.

And under no circumstances enter the fourth floor without the caretaker.

Elias had written the rules himself, though he no longer remembered why the last one mattered.

This troubled him.

His memory had once been excellent. He could identify every lost hour by its color and weight. He knew that regret produced blue smoke, while boredom condensed into gray beads. He could distinguish a moment lost to fear from one lost to indecision merely by listening to the glass that held it.

Recently, however, small things had begun to vanish from his mind.

He forgot where he kept the keys.

He forgot the name of the bakery owner, though she had brought him a burnt sugar cake every Tuesday for twenty years.

Once, while polishing a display, he caught sight of himself in the glass and needed several seconds to remember who the old man was.

The worst part was the knocking.

Every night, shortly after midnight, someone knocked three times from the other side of the fourth-floor door.

Elias always climbed the stairs carrying a lantern. He would stand in the corridor, staring at the door’s iron handle.

Knock.

Knock.

Knock.

“Who is there?” he would ask.

No one answered.

By morning, he always convinced himself it had been the pipes.

Then, one rainy Thursday, a girl named Mara Quill entered the museum.

She was perhaps twelve years old, though she spoke with the tired certainty of someone much older. Water dripped from the edge of her red coat. Under one arm she carried a wooden box.

“I need to make a donation,” she said.

Elias looked over the desk at her. “Children cannot donate time without a parent or guardian.”

“I have neither.”

“Then I am afraid you cannot donate.”

Mara placed the box on the desk. It was made of dark wood, with a brass latch and a pattern of stars carved into the lid.

“It belonged to my mother,” she said. “She told me to bring it here if she didn’t come home.”

Elias frowned. “And did she?”

“No.”

Outside, rain tapped against the windows. Somewhere in the building, a clock chimed ten, followed by another clock chiming two.

Elias reached for the box.

The instant his fingers touched the wood, something moved inside.

Not an object. A moment.

He felt it turn in the dark, restless as a sleeping bird.

“Where did your mother get this?” he asked.

“She worked here.”

Elias pulled his hand away.

“That is not possible.”

“She said you might say that.”

“What was her name?”

“Lena Quill.”

The name struck him like cold water.

For an instant he saw a woman standing on a ladder, laughing as blue sparks spilled from a cracked jar. She had black hair tied with a yellow ribbon. There was ink on her cheek. She was saying something to him.

Then the memory disappeared.

Elias gripped the edge of the desk.

“I knew her,” he whispered.

Mara studied him. “She said you would forget.”

“When did she work here?”

“I don’t know. Before I was born.”

“That was only twelve years ago. I would remember.”

“You don’t.”

Elias looked at the wooden box again. A small brass plate had been fixed to its base. He turned it over and read the engraved words.

ELIAS VALE—SEVENTH FLOOR—ONE HOUR

He dropped the box.

It struck the desk, and the latch sprang open.

The museum inhaled.

Every clock stopped.

From inside the box came the sound of waves.

Not the gentle rhythm of water against sand, but a violent sea breaking against cliffs. Wind swept through the entrance hall, carrying salt and the cry of distant birds. The lamps dimmed. The walls seemed to stretch upward.

Then, as suddenly as it had begun, the sound ceased.

Inside the box lay a single white feather.

Mara picked it up.

The museum exhaled, and every clock began ringing at once.

Elias seized the feather from her hand and shut it inside the box.

“You must leave,” he said.

“I need to find my mother.”

“Your mother left you instructions to bring the box. You have done so.”

“She also said you would take me to the seventh floor.”

Elias stared at her.

“No one goes to the seventh floor.”

“You do.”

“I have not been there in years.”

“Why?”

He opened his mouth, but no answer came.

Knock.

Knock.

Knock.

It was not midnight.

Mara looked toward the staircase. “Is that her?”

“No.”

“How do you know?”

Elias did not.

He locked the museum doors and turned the sign to CLOSED. Then he took a ring of keys from beneath the desk. There were keys of iron, keys of bone, keys so small they could be mistaken for fishhooks. At the very end hung a long black key he had never used but carried every day.

He picked up the wooden box.

“We will go as far as the fourth floor,” he said. “No farther.”

Mara smiled without amusement. “That’s what my mother said you’d say too.”

I should have—

If only—

Please forgive—

“That’s mine,” Mara said.

Elias checked the label.

MARA QUILL, AGE FIVE. ONE WINTER MORNING.

“How did it get here?” she asked.

“I didn’t forget that morning.”

“You may not have lost the memory. Perhaps someone stole the hour itself.”

Elias looked toward the stairs.

“Yes,” he said. “I believe it can.”

He knew this place.

He had stood here many times, though he had no memory of doing so.

Mara stepped onto the sand.

“Stay close,” he said.

A young man calling him Father.

Lena Quill saying, You cannot keep cutting pieces out of yourself.

“You think?”

“I can see his face, but I don’t know his name.”

“You told me the museum was more important,” the boy said.

Mara took his hand. Her fingers were cold and small, but her grip was firm.

“This place isn’t real,” she said.

“It is real enough.”

“Then we keep going.”

They reached the lighthouse.

Its door opened before them.

Inside was not a tower but a spiral staircase descending into darkness.

“The fourth floor should go up,” Mara said.

They descended.

Along the walls hung portraits covered with white cloth. As Elias passed, the cloths lifted.

“I lost these,” he said.

“No,” Mara replied. “You put them here.”

It was a railway station.

No trains arrived or departed, yet the platform was crowded with passengers made of pale smoke. They clutched suitcases and stared down empty tracks. Above them, the departure board clicked endlessly.

THINGS NEVER SAID—DELAYED  
CHANCES NOT TAKEN—CANCELLED  
LAST GOODBYES—DEPARTED  
SECOND CHANCES—UNKNOWN

FOR WHEN I HAVE FORGOTTEN ENOUGH.

Click.

Click.

Elias at eight, hiding beneath a table.

Elias at twenty, entering the museum for the first time.

Elias at thirty-seven, turning away from his son.

Elias at sixty, holding a silver instrument to his temple while Lena Quill shouted at him to stop.

He cut the hour away.

“Open the hour.”

“I will return to the moment I left.”

“You’ll come home?”

Lena looked toward the horizon.

“If the hour allows it.”

Mara’s face hardened. “That isn’t an answer.”

“It is the only one I have.”

Elias reached into the sea.

Time closed around his hand.

He remembered Jonah’s birth. His wife laughing in the garden. The unopened letters. The hospital door. Lena shouting. The years of deliberate forgetting. The pain was enormous.

The building had only three floors.

Knock.

Knock.

Knock.

Mara ran.

On the pavement stood Lena Quill.

Then Mara flung herself into Lena’s arms.

Her name was Ada Bell.

He remembered.

Other memories were returning to the city too.

A man on the pavement suddenly laughed and called his brother after twenty silent years. An old woman sat down on a doorstep as a forgotten summer afternoon bloomed in her mind. Somewhere nearby, someone began to weep for a goodbye they had denied losing.

The world had recovered its missing hours.

Not everyone would be grateful.

Lena entered the museum with Mara’s hand in hers.

“What will happen to this place?” she asked.

Elias looked around at the empty cases.

“I think the museum is closed.”

“For repairs?”

“For good.”

He stepped onto Bellweather Street with Lena and Mara. The morning smelled of rain and burnt sugar.

“Where will you go?” Mara asked him.

Elias thought of a cemetery on the northern hill. He had not visited in many years. After that, perhaps he would find Ada Bell and thank her for every cake. There were letters to read, names to relearn, and griefs to carry honestly.

“I have an appointment with my son,” he said.

Mara slipped her hand into his.

Together they walked away from the museum.

Behind them, sunlight touched the words carved above the brass doors:

WHAT IS LOST IS NOT ALWAYS GONE.

For a moment the letters shone.

Then the old building sighed, folded its impossible upper floors into the bright morning air, and became nothing more than a narrow, ordinary house at the end of the street.
